Question 10. The manuscript briefly mentions maintenance of immune tolerance (e.g.,
Line 171). A more nuanced discussion is warranted, particularly regarding the dual role
of Tregs in both suppressing inflammation and promoting fibrosis in chronic conditions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this insightful and important comment. In
the revised manuscript, we have incorporated a more nuanced discussion to clarify the
dual roles of Tregs in inflammation and fibrosis, with particular emphasis on how our
therapeutic strategy, PrEXO-a23, is designed to harness their beneficial functions while
mitigating potential risks. The key points are summarized as follows.
(1) The function of Tregs is stage-dependent: their dominant role is protective prior to
the establishment of fibrosis.
Pathological fibrosis represents a maladaptive repair outcome following sustained
chronic inflammatory injury. Throughout this process, the role of Tregs evolves
dynamically. During early disease stages and active inflammation, the core function of
Tregs is to suppress excessive immune responses and limit tissue damage, thereby
creating conditions conducive to proper repair. At this stage, expanding Tregs and
enhancing their function constitute a key protective mechanism to prevent the
progression from inflammation to fibrosis (Sci. Transl. Med. 2025, 17, eadq3516; JCI
Insight 2020, 5, e130651). Our therapy, PrEXO-a23, is designed to intervene in
inflammatory bowel disease before intestinal fibrosis develops. By simultaneously
neutralizing IL-23 (to inhibit Th17-driven inflammation) and delivering Treg-derived
exosomes (to induce immune tolerance), it fundamentally corrects the immune
dysregulation that drives fibrosis. As demonstrated in our results, PrEXO-a23 treatment
significantly upregulated the proportion of Tregs in the colon and effectively prevented
intestinal fibrosis in the fibrosis mouse model (Fig. 7l-q). This indicates that Tregs
induced at this stage primarily exert beneficial effects by suppressing inflammation and
preventing the onset of fibrosis.
(2) Treg function is tightly regulated by the local microenvironment: PrEXO-a23 shapes
a tolerogenic microenvironment that suppresses fibrosis.
Treg functionality is not fixed or cell-intrinsic but is profoundly influenced by the
surrounding microenvironment. In a milieu dominated by strong pro-inflammatory
cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-17, Tregs may be reprogrammed or lose stability,
and may even indirectly promote fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix
deposition, thereby exacerbating fibrosis. In contrast, within an immunologically
balanced or tolerogenic microenvironment, Tregs predominantly exert their classic
anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory functions (Sci. Immunol. 2022, 7, eabi4613;
Circulation 2019, 139, 206-221; J. Leukoc. Biol. 2020, 107, 573-587). The novelty of
our nanotherapeutic strategy, PrEXO-a23, lies in its ability not merely to increase the
proportion of Tregs, but to synergistically reshape the local immune microenvironment:
the a23 component effectively clears key pro-inflammatory signals such as IL-23, while
the rEXO component actively induces tolerogenic dendritic cells (tDCs) and anti-
inflammatory cytokines including IL-10. Thus, PrEXO-a23 establishes a
microenvironment that favors the anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory function of
Tregs, rather than their pro-fibrotic potential. This resembles the physiological state in
healthy individuals, where abundant Tregs are present without triggering fibrosis.
In summary, we agree that Tregs may exhibit pro-fibrotic potential in advanced disease
stages or under specific microenvironmental conditions, which is a limitation of many
current mono-modal therapies. PrEXO-a23, however, is a multi-targeted and stage-
specific combination therapy specifically designed to guide Tregs toward exerting
beneficial immunosuppressive and tolerogenic functions during the inflammatory phase,
before fibrosis occurs, thereby preemptively blocking the pathological progression to
fibrosis. Our experimental results robustly demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy.
We have incorporated a more nuanced discussion in the revised manuscript as follows.
“PrEXO-a23 mitigated fibrotic progression through a coordinated dual mechanism. By
neutralizing IL-23, it could suppress Th17-driven inflammation, while simultaneously
delivering Treg-derived exosomes to promote immune tolerance. This combined anti-
inflammatory and pro-tolerance strategy not only corrected the underlying immune
dysregulation before pathological fibrosis occurs but also reprogrammed the local
microenvironment to favor beneficial immunosuppressive and tolerogenic Treg
functions, thereby preemptively blocking the pathological progression toward fibrosis.”
Question 11. The rationale for using MMP9-responsive linkers should be clearly
introduced in the opening section. The biological significance and therapeutic relevance
of such linkers in IBD should be explicitly stated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful suggestion. We have revised the
introduction to clearly highlight the biological significance and therapeutic relevance
of such MMP9-responsive linkers.
Specifically, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP9, are highly
overexpressed and secreted by activated stromal and immune cells at inflamed
intestinal lesions in IBD (J. Crohns Colitis 2018, 12, 1011-1013). Incorporating an
MMP9-cleavable linker leverages the pathological microenvironment for controlled
drug release, thereby maximizing local therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic
exposure and off-target immunosuppression. This strategy has been validated by prior
works. For instance, MMP-mediated cleavage enabled the inflammation site–selective
release of a VEGF antibody, markedly improving its bioavailability and inhibitory
effect on neovascularization (Nat. Biomed. Eng. 2021, 5, 968-982). Similarly, a
multifunctional PROTAC nanoplatform employing an MMP-cleavable peptide was
activated by tumor-overexpressed MMP-2, leading to responsive drug release that
selectively eliminated tumor cells while reducing adverse effects (Nat. Commun. 2024,
15, 10382). In this study, we therefore employed an MMP-cleavable linker to conjugate
Treg–platelet hybrid vesicles (PrEXO) with an anti-IL-23 antibody (a23), producing
PrEXO-a23. Thus, after intravenous administration of PrEXO-a23, it selectively
accumulated at sites of damaged and inflamed colonic lesions due to platelet-mediated
damage adhesion and Treg-derived inflammation homing. Cleavage by MMPs
promoted the release of a23 and PrEXO within MMP-enriched IBD lesions, thereby
increasing local antibody bioavailability and immunomodulatory activity while
minimizing systemic exposure and off-target immunosuppression.
Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript description with the following highlighted
content:
“The introduction of an MMP9-cleavable linker can exploit the pathological
microenvironment to control drug release, thereby maximizing local therapeutic
efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target immunosuppression. Thus,
after intravenous administration of PrEXO-a23, it selectively accumulated at sites of
damaged and inflamed colonic lesions due to platelet-mediated damage adhesion and
Treg-derived inflammation homing. Cleavage by MMPs promoted the release of a23
and PrEXO within MMP-enriched IBD lesions.”

Reviewer #2: The article introduces PrEXO-a23, a novel nanotherapeutic for
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). It combines regulatory T cell (Treg)-derived
exosomes (rEXO) with platelet membrane vesicles (PMV) and uses an MMP-cleavable
linker to attach IL-23 antibodies (a23). This design leverages the homing abilities of
platelets and Treg cells to target inflamed colonic tissues in IBD mice. At the inflamed
site, MMPs release a23, which neutralizes IL-23 and inhibits Th17-mediated
inflammation. Meanwhile, rEXO reprograms dendritic cells and promotes Treg
expansion to restore immune tolerance. Tests show PrEXO-a23 reduces colitis severity,
enhances epithelial barrier integrity, rebalances the gut microbiota, and prevents
complications like intestinal fibrosis and colitis-associated colorectal cancer. Overall,
PrEXO-a23 shows potential for durable immune reprogramming and long-term
management of IBD and its complications. However, there are still a few issues that
need to be addressed:
Question 1. The material preparation section is too concise and doesn't elaborate on
determining the optimal concentrations of the binder and a23.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions. We have added a more
detailed description of the material preparation, including the optimization of the ratios
between the linker and a23, as well as between linker-a23 and PrEXO. The specific
procedures are described below.
An MMP-cleavable peptide linker (Arg-Val-Gly-Leu-Pro, RVGLP) with an NHS ester
at the Arg terminus and a 6-maleimidocaproyl (6-Mal) group at the Pro terminus was
used to conjugate an antibody (a23) to the hybrid vesicles (PrEXO). To determine the
optimal molar ratio for linker-a23 conjugation, a23 (1 mg/mL) was reacted with the
linker at molar ratios (a23: linker) of 1:1, 1:10, 1:50, 1:75, or 1:100 in PBS buffer at
4 °C for 12-18 h, forming linker-a23 via NHS-amine condensation. Unreacted linker
was removed by centrifugation at 8,000 g for 30 min using a centrifugal filter (100 kDa).
The purified linker-a23 was analyzed using matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization
time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS, AXIMA-Performance MA,
Shimadzu). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5a, the molar ratio of 1:50 (corresponding
to 1:4 w/w in the original manuscript) resulted in the highest conjugation efficiency
(∼60%).
We next optimized the mass ratio for conjugating linker-a23 to PrEXO. PrEXO was
prepared by co-extrusion of platelet membrane vesicles (PMV) and Treg-derived
exosomes (rEXO) at a 1:1 protein mass ratio, followed by protein quantification using
a BCA assay. PrEXO was treated with 1 mM tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP)
solution at 37 °C for 30 min to expose sulfhydryl (SH) groups on its membrane.
Pretreated PrEXO was then added to purified linker-a23 at a mass ratio (PrEXO: a23)
of 1:0.1 ,1:0.25, 1:0.5, 1:1, or 1:2, and incubated at 25 °C for 1 h to induce the reaction
between the SH groups of PrEXO and the 6-Mal groups of linker. Unreacted linker-a23
was removed by centrifugation at 8,000 g for 30 min using a centrifugal filter (300 kDa).
ELISA was used to determine the conjugation efficiency of a23 to PrEXO, which
showed that a PrEXO-to-a23 mass ratio of 1:0.5 provided the highest a23 conjugation
efficiency of ~30% (Supplementary Fig. 5b).
Therefore, throughout this study, a a23-to-linker molar ratio of 1:50 and a PrEXO-to-
a23 mass ratio of 1:0.5 were used to prepare the PrEXO-a23 formulations.
Supplementary Fig. 5 | Optimization of the conjugation ratios for PrEXO-a23. a, The conjugation
efficiency of linker to a23 at different molar ratio (a23: linker). b, The conjugation efficiency of a23
to PrEXO at different mass ratio (PrEXO: a23). n = 3. Data are presented as mean ± s.d.
Question 2. It's recommended that the role of Th17 cells in IBD be highlighted in the
introduction.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. We have revised the
Introduction section to highlight the pathogenic role of Th17 cells and their relevance
to our therapeutic strategy.
Specifically, Th17 cells differentiated and expanded by the cytokine IL-23, produce
proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-17A, which act on epithelial, stromal, and
immune cells to amplify inflammatory responses, disrupt epithelial barrier function,
and recruit additional immune cells to the intestinal mucosa (Nat. Rev. Gastroenterol.
Hepatol. 2023, 20, 433-446; Cell 2020, 180, 79-91). Dysregulated Th17 responses also
contribute to chronic inflammation and promote tissue remodeling, fibrosis, and colitis-
associated carcinogenesis (Nature 2006, 441, 235-238). Therefore, targeting the Th17
axis represents an important therapeutic approach in IBD. We have added the highlight
in the Introduction sections as follows.
“Th17 cells exacerbate IBD by secreting proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-17A),
which drive epithelial barrier dysfunction and chronic tissue damage, thereby
perpetuating the inflammatory cascade.”
Question 3. It's suggested that a discussion on rEXO's immune-regulating effects, such
as inhibiting Th17 cell differentiation, be included or that further experiments on its
related mechanisms be conducted.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. Treg-derived
exosomes (rEXO) are enriched in Treg-derived immunomodulatory molecules,
including proteins and miRNAs, which contribute to their function for immune
modulation (Nat. Biomed. Eng. 2021, 5, 968-982; Immunity 2014, 41, 89-103). We have
added more discussion on the immune-regulating effects of rEXO in the revised
manuscript.
In addition, we have employed proteomic analysis to confirmed that rEXO are enriched
with immunosuppressive proteins such as CTLA-4, LAG-3, IL-10, PD-L1, and TGF-
β1 (Fig. R2), suggesting its potential to suppress excessive immune activation (Acta
Biomater. 2025, 198, 452-466). We have also performed additional Western blot
validation, which indicated the abundant presence of key immunomodulatory proteins
including IL-10 and CTLA-4 in rEXO (Supplementary Fig. 2).

2025, 198, 452-466).

To investigate the regulatory effects of rEXO on Th17 cell differentiation, we
established a coculture model. Naïve CD4+ T cells were seeded in the upper chamber
and treated with IL-6 and IL-23 to induce Th17 polarization. Cells were treated with
PBS (Th17 group), rEXO (rEXO group), PMV (PMV group), PrEXO (PrEXO group),
a23 (a23 group), or PrEXO-a23 (PrEXO-a23 group), with untreated cells serving as
the negative control (Control group). Flow cytometry analysis revealed that IL-6 and
IL-23 successfully induced the differentiation of naïve T cells into Th17 cells in the Th17
group, as evidenced by an increased proportion of CD4+IL-17A+ cells compared to the
control (Fig. 3b). rEXO treatment showed effective inhibitory effects on reducing Th17
cell differentiation (P = 0.0349). Meanwhile, ELISA analysis of supernatants revealed
elevated levels of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-17A and TNF-α in the Th17 group,
consistent with Th17 activation. In contrast, rEXO treatment reduced the levels of these
cytokines (Fig. 3c, d). These results suggest that rEXO can suppress the Th17-driven
inflammation.

are presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical significance was determined using one-way ANOVA with

Given the role of Treg-derived exosomes in maintaining immune tolerance, we
evaluated whether rEXO could reprogram DCs toward a tolerogenic phenotype.
Immature DCs (imDCs) were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and IFN-γ to
induce mature DCs (mDCs) and subsequently treated with various formulations,
including PBS, rEXO, PMV, PrEXO, a23, or PrEXO-a23 for 24 h. Untreated immature
DCs (imDCs group) served as the negative control (Fig. 3f). The expression of surface
markers and cytokine profiles was analyzed using flow cytometry and ELISA,
respectively. As expected, mDCs showed increased expression of CD80, CD86, and
MHC II compared to imDCs (Fig. 3g), as well as increased production of IL-6 and
TNF-α (Fig. 3h). In contrast, rEXO treatment resulted in downregulation of maturation
markers and proinflammatory cytokines while promoting secretion of IL-10 and TGF-
β, indicating a shift toward a tolerogenic phenotype.
To further explore the potential of rEXO-induced tolerogenic DCs (tDCs) in promoting
Treg differentiation, we cocultured the pretreated mDCs with naïve T cells for 72 h, and
the phenotypes of the T cells were determined via flow cytometry (Fig. 3i). Flow
cytometry analysis revealed that PBS-treated mDCs from the mDC group did not

Question 4. The enrichment mechanism of this study deserves discussion. The material
developed in this study can be enriched in IBD lesions through the vWF factor highly
expressed in the inflamed intestine of IBD, and the targeting effectiveness has been
verified in animal models. However, in clinical settings, IBD is associated with various
extraintestinal inflammatory responses, such as skin inflammation, eye lesions, and
joint involvement. How to prevent the material from accumulating in extraintestinal
IBD lesions and whether it still has a therapeutic effect in these locations need to be
explored. Also, considering that vWF is highly expressed in many other diseases like
coronary heart disease and diabetes, how can we prevent this biomaterial from
aggregating in sites related to comorbidities with high vWF expression in patients, or
will it have a therapeutic effect after accumulation?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful questions. To address
the enrichment mechanism of PrEXO-a23, we have performed additional experiments
in relevant mouse models. Below, we outline the targeting mechanism and respond
point by point.
PrEXO-a23 achieves site-specific enrichment in IBD lesions via a synergistic dual-
targeting strategy: Treg-derived exosomes (rEXO) express high-affinity integrins that
bind to inflammation-upregulated endothelial adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1,
VCAM-1) for homing to inflamed sites (Gut 2019, 68, 1688-1700; Gut 2016, 65, 1642-
1664), while platelet membrane vesicles (PMV) enable adhesion to exposed collagen
in damaged vasculature through GPIbα-von Willebrand factor (vWF) interactions
(Nature 2015, 526, 118-121; Nat. Rev. Immunol. 2023, 23, 495-510). This combined
strategy of “inflammatory homing + damage adhesion” allows PrEXO-a23 to
preferentially accumulate in inflamed intestinal tissues, as demonstrated in our IBD
models (Fig. 4).
(1) Regarding potential accumulation and therapeutic effects in extraintestinal IBD
manifestations (e.g., skin inflammation): We developed an IBD-comorbid psoriasis
model by administering 3% DSS in drinking water and applying topical imiquimod
(IMQ) on the back skin for 7 days. DiD-labeled PrEXO-a23 was injected intravenously
into healthy (Health group) and comorbid (IBD + psoriasis group) mice, with
biodistribution monitored via an in vivo imaging. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 17,
strong fluorescence signals were observed not only in colonic lesions but also in
psoriatic skin sites in the IBD + psoriasis group mice, whereas the signals were
negligible in healthy tissues. These results confirmed that PrEXO-a23 targets
inflammation in sites beyond the colon, likely due to shared endothelial adhesion
molecules and vWF/collagen exposure in extraintestinal inflamed areas. This finding
suggests it could offer benefits for IBD comorbidities without undesired off-target
effects in non-inflamed tissues.
To assess therapeutic efficacy, IBD + psoriasis mice were grouped into PBS and
PrEXO-a23, with treatments administered intravenously every other day. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 18, compared to the PBS group (15% body weight loss, IBD
disease activity index (DAI) score ~10.2, colon length ~5.2 cm, Psoriasis DAI score
~8.0), PrEXO-a23 treatment significantly alleviated symptoms, as evidenced by 5%
weight loss, IBD score ~3.8, psoriasis score ~3.2, and colon length ~6.7 cm. These
results indicate that PrEXO-a23 not only accumulated in extraintestinal sites but also
showed therapeutic effects, possibly by modulating local inflammation and tolerance,
consistent with its dual-action design.
(2) Concerning accumulation and effects in IBD comorbidities with high vWF
expression (e.g., acute wounds): We modeled IBD-comorbid acute wounds by 3% DSS
administration and dorsal skin excision. In vivo imaging of DiD-PrEXO-a23 showed
accumulation in both colonic and wound sites in the IBD + wound group mice, with
minimal signals in healthy controls (Fig. R3), indicating that its targeting is not organ-
restricted but extends to peripheral vWF-rich or damaged vasculature, which is
attributable to PMV's collagen-binding affinity at injury sites.
While PrEXO-a23 itself is designed as an immunomodulatory agent for IBD and may
not directly match the pathophysiology of non-inflammatory conditions like acute
wounds, its strong lesion-homing capability suggests its potential utility as a targeted
delivery vehicle for combination therapies, for instance, co-loading with wound-
healing or disease-specific agents. To support this, recent studies (e.g., by Wang et al.)
have demonstrated that platelet-derived extracellular vesicles can serve as universal
carriers for inflammatory diseases including acute lung injury, atherosclerosis, and
rheumatoid arthritis, highlighting the broad applicability of inflammation-targeting
biomaterials (Matter 2020, 3, 287-301). Such studies affirm the broad utility of
inflammation/vWF-directed biomaterials, implying PrEXO-a23 can offer benefits in
IBD comorbidities without undesired off-target effects in non-inflamed tissues.
In summary, the inflammation/damage dual-targeting strategy embodied by PrEXO-
a23-based on Treg exosome and platelet membrane hybridization—enables precise
drug delivery not only to inflamed intestines but also to extraintestinal inflammatory
sites and other vWF-high pathological environments. This broader targeting capability
may offer a therapeutic advantage for IBD patients with systemic comorbidities.
We have added the new data as Supplementary Fig. 17 and 18 in the revised manuscript.

Reviewer #3: In this study, Cao et al. made a nanotherapeutic material, PrEXO-a23, to
treat inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), by fusing regulatory T cell (Treg)-derived
exosomes (rEXO) with platelet membrane vesicles, and conjugating IL-23 antibodies
(a23) via a matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-cleavable linker. Authors present in vitro
and in vivo data to show PrEXO-a23 can reduce colitis severity, rebalance gut
microbiota, and even prevent chronic complications including intestinal fibrosis and
colitis-associated colorectal cancer. However, its design has obvious defects, the key
data are not convincing and cannot support conclusions. These flaws prohibit its
publication. The following are my comments.
Major concerns:
Question 1. The design of this study highly depends on MMP activity to cleave the
linker and release anti-IL-23 antibody in inflammatory site. However, PrEXO-a23 was
injected intravenously into mice in the animal study. There are MMPs in the serum. The
anti-IL-23 antibodies could be released from PrEXO-a23 in the serum before it arrives
the inflammatory site. In addition, IL-23 level is high in the serum when the body
undergoes inflammation. The serum IL-23 will bind to anti-IL-23 antibody on PrEXO-
a23 before it arrives the inflammatory site. This study didn’t take into account MMP
and IL-23 in serum. Its design has obvious defects.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful questions.
(1) To address whether the IL-23 antibody could be released from PrEXO-a23 in the
serum before it arrives inflammatory sites, we first measured MMP9 levels in the serum
and inflamed colonic tissues of IBD mice using ELISA. As shown in Supplementary
Fig. 8c, the serum MMP9 level was ~11 ng/mL, significantly lower than that in the
inflamed colon tissue (~378 ng/mL; P < 0.0001). We further assessed the release
kinetics of PrEXO-a23 at the serum MMP9 concentration (11 ng/mL), and the results
showed that less than 3.0% of a23 was released within 2 h (Fig. R4). Given the short
circulatory half-life of PrEXO-a23 (1.44 h; Supplementary Fig. 13c), the low MMP9 in
the blood results in negligible a23 release.
Additionally, we performed a dual-label in vivo tracking study to independently
monitor the distribution of the antibody (a23) and the carrier (PrEXO). As demonstrated
in Fig. 4h, PrEXO-a23 showed strong and sustained accumulation of a23 signals in the
colonic lesions of IBD mice. These results further confirmed that the IL-23 antibody
was not prematurely released before reaching the inflammatory site.

due to inflammation. In contrast, the PrEXO-a23 group showed a substantial reduction

Question 3. Figure 2e, authors said that “The rEXO and PMV were then fused through
additional coextrusion to generate hybrid vesicles (PrEXO).” Therefore, PrEXO should
contain both exosomal and platelet markers. However, Figure 2e show that PrEXO has

TSG101, and CCR6, as well as GPIbα and CD62P. Weirdly, PrEXO, without the
conjugation of anti-IL-23 antibody, shows the presence of anti-IL-23 antibody (a23).
One more problem is the molecular weight of a23. a23 is a monoclonal rat antibody. It
should have light and heavy chain. Light chain is around 24kDa. Heavy chain is around
55kDa. The whole IgG molecule is around 150 kDa. When performing western blot,
IgG antibody will disassemble. Only light and heavy chain appear in the gel at around
25kDa and 55kDa. The 150kDa antibody cannot be detected. The 150kDa band in
Figure 2e is not a23. Overall, this western blot demonstrates that PrEXO is wrong and
the presence of anti-IL-23 antibody in PrEXO-a23 is suspicious.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these professional comments.
(1) Regarding the original Fig. 2e, the lane originally labeled as “PrEXO” did not show
bands corresponding to exosomal proteins (ALIX, TSG101, and CCR6) or platelet
markers (GPIbα and CD62P) but instead showed the presence of the IL-23 antibody
(~150 kDa). After careful review, the lane labeled as “PrEXO” should be “IL-23
antibody (a23)”, we apologize for this error and have corrected them in the revised
figure as shown in Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 7.
(2) Regarding the concern about the molecular weight of the IL-23 antibody (a23), we
agree with the reviewer that under general Western blot conditions, which utilize
reducing agents such as DTT and β-mercaptoethanol, IgG antibodies undergo disulfide
bond reduction, resulting in dissociation into light (~25 kDa) and heavy chains (~50-55
kDa), thereby preventing detection of the full-length ~150 kDa immunoglobulin. In this
study, we employed an alternative immunodetection system, a fully automated Digital
Capillary Electrophoresis-Western (CE-Western) platform for protein detection. This
automated CE technology uses proprietary-coated capillaries to perform size-based
separation, immobilization, immunoprobing, and detection in a single, integrated
process. Critically, samples were prepared without reducing agents, enabling analysis
under non-reducing conditions. This preserves the native quaternary structure of
antibodies, allowing the a23 antibody (IgG monoclonal antibody) to migrate at its intact
molecular weight of ~150 kDa. The CE-Western method is well established and has
been extensively validated in peer-reviewed studies for accurate analysis of proteins in
native or semi-native states (Nat. Biomed. Eng. 2021, 5, 968-982; Nature 2025, 638,
1095-1103; Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 7375).
We sincerely apologize for the lack of detailed methods in our original manuscript. We
have now added a detailed description of the Digital CE-Western system to the Methods
section and, crucially, have explicitly stated that the analysis was performed under non-
reducing conditions.

(and references therein).

induced colitis described by you and Hartl et al. (Sci. Adv 2024, adp8783), and the

these elevated proteins returned to levels comparable to those in healthy mice, which
may be attributed to its anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, thereby
effectively protecting intestinal cells and alleviating acute cellular damage.
Furthermore, we evaluated the expression of Trp53 and its downstream target genes
(Cdkn1a and Bax) using RT-qPCR. The results showed that Trp53, Cdkn1a, and Bax
mRNA were significantly downregulated in the DSS group compared with healthy mice.
Notably, PrEXO-a23 treatment also upregulated the expression of these genes to levels
similar to those in the healthy group (Fig. R9). Our results, as well as those from the
references confirm that the p53 signaling pathway plays a key role in IBD, which is
consistent with our core conclusion.
To further demonstrate whether PrEXO-a23 can suppress CAC by regulating the p53
signaling pathway, we collected colonic tissue from mice with AOM/DSS-induced
CAC and analyzed the expression of p53 and its downstream target factors using RT-
qPCR and Western blot. RT-qPCR results showed that compared with healthy mice,
mRNA levels of Trp53 and its target genes, Cdkn1a (which promotes cell cycle arrest)
and Bax (which promotes apoptosis) were significantly downregulated in the
AOM/DSS group. However, PrEXO-a23 treatment upregulated their expression (Fig.
8h). However, this restorative effect was abolished by p53 inhibition (PrEXO-a23 +
ip53). We further examined the protein expression of p53, p21, and Bax. As shown in
Fig. 8i, j, compared to the AOM/DSS group, PrEXO-a23 treatment upregulated the
expression of p53, p21, and Bax, restoring them to levels comparable to the healthy
group. These results indicate that PrEXO-a23 inhibits CAC by regulating the p53
signaling pathway.

colonic tissues of IBD mice with indicated treatment. n = 5 mice. Data are presented as mean ± s.d.
Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
Fig. R9 | Relative mRNA expression levels of Trp53, Cdkn1a, and Bax in colonic tissues of IBD
mice with indicated treatment measured by RT-qPCR assay. n = 5 mice. Data are presented as mean
± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple
comparisons test.

mice with indicated treatment measured by RT-qPCR assay. n = 5 mice. Data are presented as mean
± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple

Question 2. Throughout, please use correct nomenclature for murine genes and proteins.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this kind suggestion. We have corrected them in
the revised manuscript.
Question 3 Page 6. “Cells were treated with PBS, rEXO, PMV, PrEXO, a23, or PrEXO-
a23, with untreated cells serving as controls” It is not mentioned whether PMV
produced any effect. This would serve as additional control.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's thoughtful suggestion. We have revised the
relevant paragraphs in the Results section according to your suggestions.
To investigate the regulatory effects of PrEXO-a23 on Th17 cell differentiation and its
potential to protect intestinal epithelial cells, we established a coculture model. Naïve
CD4+ T cells were seeded in the upper chamber and treated with IL-6 and IL-23 to
induce Th17 polarization. Cells were treated with PBS (Th17 group), rEXO (rEXO
group), PMV (PMV group), PrEXO (PrEXO group), a23 (a23 group), or PrEXO-a23
(PrEXO-a23 group), with untreated cells serving as the negative control (Control
group). After 72 h of treatment, colonic epithelial NCM460 cells were seeded into the
lower chamber and cocultured with the pretreated T cells for an additional 24 h to
evaluate the epithelial response (Fig. 3a).
Flow cytometry analysis revealed that IL-6 and IL-23 successfully induced the
differentiation of naïve T cells into Th17 cells in the Th17 group, as evidenced by an
increased proportion of CD4+IL-17A+ cells compared to the Control group (Fig. 3b).
Compared with the Th17 group, PMV treatment had no inhibitory effects on Th17 cell
differentiation. Meanwhile, ELISA analysis of supernatants revealed elevated levels of
the proinflammatory cytokines IL-17A and TNF-α in the Th17 group, consistent with
Th17 activation. There was no significant difference in the secretion of these
inflammatory cytokines in the PMV group (Fig. 3c, d).
We next examined the effects of Th17 polarization on epithelial cell viability. The results
showed that apoptosis and necrosis of NCM460 cells were significantly increased when
co-cultured with Th17 cells in the Th17 group (P < 0.0001), indicating epithelial cell
damage. Similarly, PMV alone had minimal protective effect against Th17-induced
epithelial damage (Fig. 3e). These findings collectively demonstrate that PMV has no
significant regulatory effect on Th17-driven inflammatory responses.
Fig. 3a-e | a, Experimental schema of the co-culture system between naïve T cells and NCM460
cells. b, Flow cytometric quantification of Th17 cells (CD4+ IL-17A+) in CD4+ T cells. c, d, ELISA
analysis of IL-17A (c) and TNF-α (d) levels in CD4+ T cell culture supernatants. e, Flow cytometric
quantification of apoptotic rate in NCM460 cells. n = 4. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical
significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
Question 4 “We next examined the effects of Th17 polarization on epithelial viability.”
The experiments are on cells, not epithelium.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s suggestion. We have revised the text as follows.
“We next examined the effects of Th17 polarization on epithelial cell viability.”
Question 5 Page 7. “The immature DCs (imDCs) were activated with
lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and IFN-γ to induce maturation and subsequently treated with
various formulations, including PBS, rEXO, PMV, PrEXO, a23 or PrEXO-a23 for 24
h.” Also here nothing is said re results with PMV.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion.
Given the role of Treg-derived exosomes in maintaining immune tolerance, we
evaluated whether PrEXO-a23 could reprogram mature DCs (mDCs) toward a
tolerogenic phenotype. The immature DCs (imDCs) were stimulated with
lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and IFN-γ to induce mDCs and subsequently treated with
various formulations, including PBS, rEXO, PMV, PrEXO, a23 or PrEXO-a23 for 24
h. Untreated immature DCs (imDCs group) served as the negative control (Fig. 3f). The
expression of surface markers and cytokine profiles were analyzed using flow cytometry
and ELISA, respectively. As expected, mDCs showed increased expression of CD80,
CD86, and MHC II compared to imDCs (Fig. 3g), as well as increased production of
IL-6 and TNF-α (Fig. 3h). PMV treatment did not significantly affect these markers or
cytokines on mDCs.
To further explore the potential of PrEXO-a23-induecd DCs in promoting Treg
differentiation, we cocultured the pretreated DCs with naïve T cells for 72 h, and the
phenotypes of the T cells were determined via flow cytometry (Fig. 3i). Flow cytometry
analysis revealed that mDCs from the mDCs group did not significantly induce Treg
differentiation compared to imDCs (P = 0.9998; Fig. 3j). Likewise, PMV-treated mDCs
failed to promote Treg differentiation (Fig. 3j), and showed a negligible effect on the
proportion of Th17 (CD4+ IL-17A+) cells (Fig. 3k). Collectively, these results indicate
that PMV does not induce immune tolerance under these conditions.
Fig. 3f-h | f, Experimental schema of the shift of mDCs into tDCs. g, Flow cytometry analysis of
the expression of CD80/CD86 and MHC II in CD11c+ cells for DCs. h, ELISA analysis of IL-6,
TNF-α, IL-10, and TGF-β in supernatant of DCs. n = 5. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical
significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
Fig. 3i-k | i, Experimental schema of T cell differentiation assay in naïve T cells co-cultured with
pretreated DCs, analyzed using flow cytometry. j, k, Polarization of Tregs (CD25+ FOXP3+) (j) and
Th17 (CD4+ IL-17A+) cells (k) in CD4+ T cells. n = 5. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical
significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
Question 6 Page 10 “These therapeutic effects likely result from the hybrid membrane-
mediated lesion targeting, which delivers a23 to locally inhibit the IL-23/Th17 axis,
combined with PrEXO’s role as an immune tolerance modulator to regulate the
inflammatory microenvironment” The anti-inflammatory agents within rEXO’s should
be described. Any measurements that they contained the expected molecules?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion. Treg-derived
exosomes (rEXO) are indeed enriched in a variety of immunomodulatory molecules,
including proteins and miRNAs, which contribute to their immunomodulatory
functions (Nat. Biomed. Eng. 2021, 5, 968-982; Immunity 2014, 41, 89-103).
To address this point, we have performed proteomic analysis to confirm that rEXO
carried multiple immunosuppressive proteins, such as CTLA-4, LAG-3, IL-10, PD-L1,
and TGF-β1, suggesting their potential to suppress excessive immune activation (Fig.
R10; Acta Biomater. 2025, 198, 452-466).
We also performed additional Western blot validation, and the results clearly showed
that rEXO were enriched in key immunoregulatory proteins such as IL-10 and CTLA-
4 (Supplementary Fig. 2). These results directly demonstrate that rEXO contain the
expected immunosuppressive molecules, likely contributing to their therapeutic effects.
Fig. R10 | The relative abundance of CTLA-4, LAG-3, IL-10, PD-L1, and TGF-β1 in rEXO and
IL-6-treated rEXO using proteomic analysis. n = 4. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. (Acta Biomater.
2025, 198, 452-466).
Supplementary Fig. 2 | Western blot analysis of IL-10 and CTLA-4 in rEXO using automated
Digital CE-Western system.
Question 7 Page 11. “Although PrEXO showed Although PrEXO showed some
potential to induce Tregs and suppress Th17 cells in vitro,”
Please delete extra words
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the typographical error. We have
corrected them in the revised manuscript.
Question 8 Page 12. “Mice received 3% (w/v) DSS in drinking water for 7 days,
followed by daily intravenous treatments as outlined in Fig. 6a.” Confusing timeline in
text.
Response: We apologize for this confusion. We have revised the description in the
manuscript as follows.
“Mice received 3% (w/v) DSS in drinking water for 7 days. Meanwhile, mice were
treated on days 2, 4, and 6 by intravenous administration, as outlined in Fig. 6a.”
Fig. 6a | Experimental design for evaluating the therapeutic effect of PrEXO-a23 in the IBD mouse
model.
Question 9 Page 13. “We next investigated microbiota modulation by PrEXO-a23 in
IBD mice via 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene sequencing of fecal samples.” Is it
unexpected to see these changes after eight days?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point.
Inflammation rapidly alters the intestinal physicochemical environment (e.g., oxidative
state and nitrate levels) and compromises epithelial integrity, thereby imposing
selective pressures that favor the expansion of inflammation-adapted pathobionts and
suppress beneficial commensals. Such changes ultimately lead to functional disruption
of the microbiota in IBD (Science, 2013, 339, 708-711; Gut Microbes. 2024, 16,
2361493).
Our results demonstrated that PrEXO-a23 functioned synergistically through two
mechanisms. First, it alleviated intestinal inflammation by targeting and neutralizing
IL-23, inhibiting Th17 cell differentiation, and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Second, it actively promoted immune tolerance by inducing tolerogenic dendritic cells
and regulatory T cells. Restoration of immune balance was accompanied by significant
improvement in epithelial barrier function. With reduced inflammation and restored
barrier integrity, the pathological colonic microenvironment was effectively reversed,
inhibiting pathogenic bacterial overgrowth and promoting overall microbiome
restoration. Thus, the changes we observed after 8 days of treatment are appropriate
and highlight the effectiveness of PrEXO-a23 in rapidly reshaping the intestinal
ecosystem through integrated immune and barrier regulation. These effects are
consistent with previous findings in DSS-induced IBD models, in which interventions
targeting inflammation or barrier repair have been shown to induce detectable
microbiota changes within 7 to 10 days (Nat. Mater. 2020, 19, 118-126; Nat. Commun.
2025, 16, 3365; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1333; Nat. Rev. Immunol. 2016, 16, 295-309).
Point-by-point responses to Reviewers
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): Comments: The revised manuscript has
satisfactorily addressed the majority of the concerns previously raised by this reviewer.
Only a few minor points remain for further consideration:
Question 1. Supplementary Fig. 13b: It would be valuable to include a more intuitive
comparison of fluorescence intensity specifically at the colon site. As the
biodistribution profiles across the four groups show negligible differences in the liver,
presenting a higher target-to-non-target ratio (e.g., colon/liver) could better emphasize
the targeting efficacy of the system.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. According to your
suggestion, we have supplemented the ex vivo colon fluorescence data and calculated
the per-animal target-to-non-target ratio (colon/liver radiant efficiency). As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 13c-e, although the fluorescence intensity of liver was comparable
across groups, the colon/liver ratios for both PrEXO and PrEXO-a23 were significantly
higher than for rEXO, PMV, and the physical mixture (P < 0.05). These data support
our conclusion that membrane fusion synergistically enhances the targeting efficacy of
PrEXO-a23 toward colonic lesions.
Supplementary Fig. 13c-e | c, Representative ex vivo fluorescence images of major organs
(heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and colon) collected from IBD mice following injection of
DiD-labeled formulations. d, Quantitative analysis of fluorescence radiant efficiency for each
harvested organ. e, Colon-to-liver ratio of fluorescence radiant efficiency. n = 3 mice. Data are
presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with
Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
Question 2. Supplementary Fig. 8c: Direct comparison between the concentration
obtained from colon tissue homogenates and that from plasma is not recommended.
The concentration in tissue homogenates inherently depends on the dilution factor
introduced by the PBS volume used during homogenization; thus, it is not directly
comparable to the concentration measured in serum.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for raising this important point. To
address this concern, we have reanalyzed the data using protein concentration
normalization. Specifically, we determined the total protein concentrations in colon
tissue homogenates and plasma samples using the BCA assay, which were ~1.12
mg/mL (for colon tissue homogenates prepared with 90 μL PBS per 1 mg tissue) and
~5.01 mg/mL (for plasma), respectively. The MMP9 concentrations were then
normalized to nanograms per milligram of total protein (ng/mg). After normalization,
the MMP9 concentration in colon tissue was 338 ng/mg (378 ng/mL ÷ 1.12 mg/mL =
338 ng/mL), while that in plasma was 2.2 ng/mg (11 ng/mL ÷ 5.01 mg/mL = 2.2 ng/mL).
The updated results are presented in Supplementary Fig. 8c. This normalized analysis
demonstrates that the MMP9 concentration in plasma is significantly lower than that in
colon tissue (P < 0.0001), thereby more reliably confirming our original findings.
Supplementary Fig. 8c | MMP9 concentrations in serum and colonic lesion of IBD mice
measured by ELISA and normalized to total protein. n = 5 mice. Data are presented as mean ±
s.d. Statistical significance was determined by Student's t-test (two-tailed).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author): Thank you for submitting the revised manuscript
and for your detailed responses to the reviewers’ comments. I have carefully reviewed
the revised version and the authors’ point-by-point replies. The authors have addressed
all reviewers’ previous concerns thoroughly and made substantial improvements to the
manuscript. I believe this work is suitable for publication in its current form.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the kind words and thoughtful
evaluation of our revised manuscript. Your positive feedback on the manuscript is
highly valued. Thank you again for your time and insightful feedback.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): This is a revised version of the study by Cao et
al "Engineered exosome nanovesicles efficiently deliver antibodies in vivo to treat
inflammatory bowel disease". Much of this work is outside my field and I was pleased
to see three other expert reviewers tackling the task. I can see that the authors have gone
through significant effort in order to address all comments. My main concern, however,
was the claimed mechanism, originally described as “Notably, PrEXO-a23 treatment
also upregulates the expression of the tumor suppressor gene p53, further enhancing
protection against inflammation-driven carcinogenesis.” The additional data is not that
helpful in view of this claim. As might have been expected through previous literature,
the inflammation itself increases Trp53 protein expression, and probably the respective
pathway. This effect is then reduced after the treatment. It is difficult to say what causes
this reduction; whether e.g. it is just a bystander effect of easing inflammation.
Nevertheless, it is of course interesting that the protein level decreases. But then, Trp53
mRNA levels increase after PrEXO-a23 treatment. What would be the purpose of that?
Taken together, the evidence and story could be more robust. It might be wise to leave
the mechanism open.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful comments, which have
been instrumental in refining our mechanistic interpretation.
As is known, p53 is a crucial tumor suppressor that maintains cellular homeostasis by
regulating cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and DNA repair (Gastroenterology 2022, 162,
715–730; Nat Commun 2023, 14, 110). In IBD, excessive p53 activation can drive
epithelial cell death and exacerbate tissue injury (Sci Adv 2024, adp8783), while loss or
dysfunction of p53 serves as an established early driver of colitis-associated colorectal
carcinogenesis (Cancer Cell 2013, 23, 634-646; Nat Cancer 2024, 5, 983-995; Nat
Genet 2023, 55, 1531–1541). Therefore, therapeutic benefit derives not from simply
increasing or decreasing p53 expression, but from maintaining homeostasis of the p53
signaling pathway. Both chronic loss of p53 and uncontrolled acute hyperactivation are
detrimental, whereas homeostasis of p53 signaling confers protection (Cell 2009, 140:
384-396).
The mRNA-protein discordance is frequently observed for p53, which can be attributed
to the fact that p53 expression is a highly dynamic process governed by multiple
complex regulatory factors (Cancer Cell 2024, 42:946-967): (i) Post-translational
modifications: Inflammation-induced phosphorylation or acetylation can stabilize p53
protein, leading to its accumulation despite unchanged or decreased mRNA levels
(Signal Transduct Target Ther 2020, 5, 90; Cancer Cell 2024, 42:946-967). (ii)
Negative feedback mechanisms: Immune interventions can modulate the MDM2-
mediated ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, leading to rapid clearance in p53 protein
levels that are independent of its mRNA abundance (Nat Rev Cancer 2020, 20, 471-
480.). These mechanisms may collectively account for the frequent discordance
between p53 mRNA and protein levels.
To investigate the effect of PrEXO-a23 on p53 pathway in IBD, we performed Western
blot analysis on colon tissues from a DSS-induced IBD model. Western blot analysis
revealed that compared with healthy controls, the IBD mice exhibited a significant
increase in p53 protein levels, along with elevated expression of its downstream targets
p21 and Bax (Fig. R1), indicating aberrant p53 activation in IBD. Following PrEXO-
a23 treatment, these elevated protein levels returned to levels comparable to those in
healthy mice, demonstrating that PrEXO-a23 helps maintain homeostasis of the p53
signaling pathway. Additionally, RT‑qPCR analysis showed downregulation of Trp53,
Cdkn1a, and Bax mRNA in IBD mice relative to healthy controls (Fig. R2). Notably,
PrEXO-a23 treatment maintained the expression levels of these genes to those observed
in the healthy group. Collectively, these data indicate that PrEXO-a23 contributes to
the maintenance of p53 signaling homeostasis in IBD.
We further evaluated the anti-CAC efficacy of PrEXO-a23 in an AOM/DSS-induced
CAC mouse model. PrEXO-a23 treatment completely inhibited tumor formation,
demonstrating its potent anti-carcinogenic effect and capacity to halt IBD-to-CAC
progression. Mice were then co-treated with the p53 inhibitor. This intervention
markedly diminished the therapeutic efficacy of PrEXO-a23 and negated its anti-tumor
effects (Fig. 8a-g), supporting that the anti-tumor action of PrEXO-a23 is at least
partially p53-dependent. Furthermore, we analyzed the expression of p53 and its
downstream targets in colon tissues from CAC mice using RT‑qPCR and Western blot.
Compared with the healthy control group, Trp53 mRNAs were decreased, and Cdkn1a
and Bax were downregulated in the CAC mice, suggesting dysfunction of the p53
pathway during CAC progression. Notably, treatment with PrEXO‑a23 maintained
their expression (Trp53/Cdkn1a/Bax) to near-normal levels (Fig. 8h). However, this
maintenance was abolished upon p53 inhibition. Western blot results confirmed these
changes in the levels of p53, p21, and Bax proteins (Fig. 8i, j). These findings suggest
that PrEXO‑a23 treatment contributes to the maintenance of p53 signaling homeostasis,
with the potential to reduce the risk of progression from IBD to CAC.
Based on your feedback and our experimental data, we think that the action of PrEXO-
a23 cannot be simply characterized as “up-regulating” or “down-regulating” p53, but
contributes to the maintenance of p53 pathway homeostasis. p53 pathway homeostasis
plays a critical role in anti-tumor efficacy. Accordingly, we have revised the initial
statement, “Notably, PrEXO-a23 treatment also upregulates the expression of the tumor
suppressor gene p53, further enhancing protection against inflammation-driven
carcinogenesis.” to the more scientifically rigorous conclusion: “Notably, PrEXO-a23
treatment also contributes to the maintenance of p53 signaling homeostasis, with the
potential to reduce the risk of progression from IBD to CAC.”
Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript as follows.
Abstract section: “Notably, PrEXO-a23 treatment also contributes to the maintenance
of p53 signaling homeostasis, with the potential to reduce the risk of progression from
IBD to CAC.”
Introduction section: “Notably, PrEXO-a23 contributes to the maintenance of p53
signaling homeostasis, which potentially further inhibited CAC development (Fig. 1).”
Result section: “To evaluate the long-term therapeutic potential of PrEXO-a23 in
preventing IBD-associated complications such as intestinal fibrosis and CAC, we
employed an AOM/DSS-induced CAC mouse model. Mice were administered AOM
followed by repeated cycles of DSS to induce chronic colitis and tumorigenesis, with
untreated healthy mice serving as controls (Health group). During disease progression,
mice received intravenous injections of PBS (AOM/DSS group), PrEXO (PrEXO group),
a23 (a23 group), rEXO-a23 (rEXO-a23 group) or PrEXO-a23 (PrEXO-a23 group)
(Fig. 7b). As expected, AOM/DSS-treated mice exhibited significantly reduced survival
(P = 0.0208; Fig. 7c), substantial weight loss (Supplementary Fig. 21a), and
significantly elevated DAI scores (Fig. 7d), shortened colon length, and increased
tumor burden, both in terms of number and size (Fig. 7e-g and Supplementary Fig. 21b).
Among all treatment groups, PrEXO-a23 demonstrated the robust therapeutic efficacy,
markedly improving survival, body weight, DAI, and colon morphology to levels
comparable with healthy controls. Importantly, while PrEXO, a23, and rEXO-a23
treatments conferred partial protection, none of these monotherapies prevented tumor
development. In contrast, PrEXO-a23 treatment completely inhibited tumor formation,
highlighting its potent anti-carcinogenic effect and capacity to halt IBD-to-CAC
progression.
We previously demonstrated that PrEXO-a23 affected the Trp53 expression change in
DSS-treated colons. Mice were co-treated with the p53 inhibitor pifithrin-α. This
intervention markedly diminished the therapeutic efficacy of PrEXO-a23 and negated
its anti-tumor effects (Fig. 8a-g), further supporting that the action of PrEXO-a23 in
preventing CAC progression is at least partially dependent on p53. Notably, the p53
pathway plays a crucial role in tumor suppression, with a mechanism involving various
factors such as Cdkn1a/p21 and Bax. Therefore, we investigated the expression of p53,
Cdkn1a/p21, and Bax in colonic tissues using RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis.
Compared with the health control group, Trp53 mRNAs were decreased, and Cdkn1a
and Bax were downregulated in the AOM/DSS group, suggesting dysfunction of the p53
pathway during CAC progression. Notably, treatment with PrEXO‑a23 maintained
their expression (Trp53/Cdkn1a/Bax) to near-normal levels (Fig. 8h). However, this
maintenance was abolished upon p53 inhibition (PrEXO‑a23 + ip53). Western blot
results confirmed these changes in the levels of p53, p21, and Bax proteins (Fig. 8i, j).
These findings suggest that PrEXO‑a23 treatment contributes to the maintenance of
p53 signaling homeostasis, with the potential to reduce the risk of progression from
IBD to CAC. Collectively, PrEXO-a23 not only attenuates active inflammation but also
provides durable protection against fibrosis and tumorigenesis, highlighting it as a
promising therapeutic strategy for the long-term management of IBD and its
complications.”
Conclusion section: “Additionally, it contributes to the maintenance of p53 signaling
homeostasis, potentially reducing the risk of progression from IBD to CAC.”
Fig. R1 | Western blot images and relative protein level analysis of p53, p21, and Bax expressed
in colonic tissues of IBD mice with indicated treatment. n = 5 mice. Data are presented as mean
± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple
comparisons test.
Fig. R2 | Relative mRNA expression levels of Trp53, Cdkn1a, and Bax in colonic tissues of
IBD mice with indicated treatment measured by RT-qPCR assay. n = 5 mice. Data are presented
as mean ± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's
multiple comparisons test.
Fig. 8h | Relative mRNA expression levels of Trp53, Cdkn1a, and Bax in colonic tissues of
CAC mice with indicated treatment measured by RT-qPCR assay. n = 5 mice. Data are
presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with
Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
Fig. 8i, j | Western blot images (i) and relative protein level analysis (j) of p53, p21, and Bax
expressed in colonic tissues. n = 3 mice. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Statistical
significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test.

## Paper

## Abstract

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is characterized by chronic inflammation and impaired immune tolerance, for which current therapies provide only partial and transient relief. Here, we introduce PrEXO-a23, a biomimetic nanotherapeutic engineered by fusing regulatory T cell (Treg)-derived exosomes with platelet membrane vesicles and conjugating interleukin-23 (IL-23) antibodies via a matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-cleavable linker. This design exploits the inherent homing ability of platelets and Tregs, enabling PrEXO-a23 to preferentially accumulate in inflamed colonic tissues in murine IBD models. At the disease site, elevated MMP activity triggers antibody release to inhibit IL-23-mediated inflammation, while exosomal cargo reprograms dendritic cells and promotes Treg expansion, thereby restoring immune tolerance. This dual-action strategy significantly alleviates IBD, prevents complications like intestinal fibrosis and colitis-associated colorectal cancer, and shows p53-dependent efficacy in carcinogenesis prevention. These findings highlight PrEXO-a23 as a promising nanotherapeutic platform for durable immune reprogramming and long-term IBD management.

---

## Introduction

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic relapsing gastrointestinal disorder characterized by debilitating symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding, which often progress to life-threatening complications1. A key driver of IBD pathogenesis is sustained intestinal inflammation coupled with impaired immune tolerance, leading to a vicious cycle of immune dysregulation2,3. Although current treatments, including probiotics, small-molecule medicines, immunosuppressants, and biologics, can reduce disease symptoms, their efficacy in reversing immune dysregulation remains limited4–6. Critically, unresolved immune imbalance increases the risk of disease relapse and contributes to progressive complications such as intestinal fibrosis and colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC). Intestinal fibrosis is characterized by thickened intestinal walls and reduced peristalsis, eventually leading to intestinal stenosis and life-threatening obstruction. The cumulative incidence of intestinal fibrosis is reported as >50% in CD and 2–11% in UC7,8. In parallel, chronic immune dysregulation promotes somatic mutations in intestinal epithelial cells, including key tumor suppressor genes such as TP53, driving the progression to CAC. Patients with IBD have an ~2–3-fold increased risk of developing CAC compared to the general population9–11. Despite this, there are currently no FDA-approved treatments for intestinal fibrosis8, and CAC remains associated with poor clinical outcomes11. Therefore, there is an urgent need for therapeutic strategies that not only suppress inflammation but also restore immune tolerance to correct immune dysregulation, with the goal of reducing disease severity and long-term complications.

The proinflammatory cytokine interleukin-23 (IL-23) plays a central role in the pathogenesis of IBD by promoting the differentiation, expansion, and effector function of T-helper 17 (Th17) cells12. Th17 cells exacerbate IBD by secreting proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-17A), which drive epithelial barrier dysfunction and chronic tissue damage, thereby perpetuating the inflammatory cascade13,14. Therapeutic antibodies targeting IL-23 specifically neutralize these cytokines, effectively disrupting the inflammatory cascade and reducing disease symptoms. Clinical studies have shown that IL-23 antibodies achieve remission rates of ~40%, substantially outperforming conventional therapies, which typically yield remission rates below 20%15,16. However, systemic administration of IL-23 antibodies may lead to off-target immunosuppression, increasing the risk of opportunistic infections17. Consequently, the development of targeted delivery systems is essential to enhance therapeutic safety and improve treatment efficacy.

Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are crucial for maintaining immune tolerance18,19, making Treg-based therapies promising candidates for IBD treatment, as supported by ongoing clinical and preclinical studies20–22. However, the direct application of Tregs is challenged by complex isolation and expansion protocols, as well as their reduced stability within the inflammatory microenvironment14,23. As an alternative, exosomes derived from Tregs have emerged as potent immunomodulatory nanovesicles. These nanoscale vesicles carry diverse functional biomolecules, including cytokines, microRNAs, and proteins, that facilitate immune regulation by targeting and reprogramming recipient immune cells24,25. Importantly, rEXO therapy bypasses the stability issues associated with cell-based Treg therapy, making it a compelling strategy for modulating immune tolerance in IBD.

The pathological features of IBD include an inflammatory environment and damaged intestinal vasculature26,27. High-affinity integrins that bind inflammation-upregulated endothelial adhesion molecules are expressed on the Treg cell surface, enabling the targeting of inflamed lesions28,29. Platelets, which possess unique surface molecules (e.g., GPIbα), can preferentially localize to damaged vasculature through robust adhesion to collagen exposed on the injured vascular endothelium30,31. The platelet-Treg hybrid engineering strategy offers an approach for enabling lesion-specific drug delivery through a dual-targeting mechanism for IBD therapy.

Inspired by these findings, we engineered a platelet-Treg hybrid nanovesicle system (PrEXO-a23) for lesion-specific delivery of anti-inflammatory and immune tolerance agents to address immune dysregulation for IBD treatment. rEXO was fused with platelet membrane vesicles (PMV) to generate hybrid nanovesicles (PrEXO), followed by the conjugation of IL-23 antibodies (a23) via a matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-cleavable peptide linker. MMPs are overexpressed and released by activated stromal cells and immune cells infiltrating the inflamed intestinal mucosa in IBD32. The introduction of an MMP9-cleavable linker can exploit the pathological microenvironment to control drug release, thereby maximizing local therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target immunosuppression24,33. Thus, after intravenous administration of PrEXO-a23, it selectively accumulated at sites of damaged and inflamed colonic lesions due to platelet-mediated damage adhesion and Treg-derived inflammation homing. Cleavage by MMPs promoted the release of a23 and PrEXO within MMP-enriched IBD lesions. The release of a23 neutralized the cytokine IL-23, which suppressed inflammation, while the PrEXO, enriched with immunomodulatory molecules from Tregs, reprogrammed local immune cells into regulatory phenotypes, such as tolerogenic dendritic cells (tDCs) and Tregs, promoting immune tolerance. As a result, in murine IBD models, PrEXO-a23 treatment effectively modulated colonic immune dysregulation, leading to comprehensive IBD remission, including symptom relief, intestinal barrier repair, and microbiota normalization. Furthermore, PrEXO-a23 significantly decreased the risk of complications, such as intestinal fibrosis and CAC. Notably, the action of PrEXO-a23 to prevent CAC progression is partially dependent on p53 (Fig. 1).
